69212.etyen:
Inherited from Middle Norwegian vera (“to be”), from Old Norse vera, earlier vesa, from Proto-Germanic *wesaną (“to be”). The infinitive and past-tense stem continue Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“to dwell; stay”). The present tense er, from Old Norse er, earlier es, belongs to the suppletive present-tense paradigm ultimately inherited from Proto-Indo-European *h₁es- (“to be”).
Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vere, Danish være, Swedish vara, Icelandic vera, Faroese vera, Dutch wezen (“to be”), and English was and were. / Inherited from Old Norse viðra (“to blow; scent”), from Proto-Germanic *wedrōną (“to expose to the weather”), a derivative of Proto-Germanic *wedrą (“weather”), whose further origin is uncertain. Related to vær (“weather”).
Cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk vêre, Danish vejre (“to scent”), Swedish vädra (“to air; scent”), Icelandic viðra (“to air; ventilate”), and German wettern (“to storm; rant”).

Borrowed from French plantage (“planting; planted area”), formed from planter (“to plant”) + -age (“action/result-forming noun suffix”). The French verb is from Latin plantāre (“to press or tamp earth with the foot; to plant”), from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”). The French noun originally denoted the action of planting and subsequently, by metonymy, an area which had been planted.

The character was adopted with the Latin alphabet into medieval Scandinavian writing and used to represent native front unrounded vowels. 1001820.etyen:
A fixed phrase consisting of the imperative ha (“to have”), the pronoun det (“it”) and adverbial bra (“well”), literally “have it well”. As a farewell, the phrase is an imperative wish that the addressee continue to be well. The shortened farewell ha det (“goodbye, bye”) is an ellipsis of this expression or ha det godt (“goodbye, take care”).
